title: what the string is for
hook: beads on a rearview mirror: counting, not magic

segments.voice: Yesterday: confession, the thing said out loud. Today, something that might be hanging from a rearview mirror near you.

A loop of beads swinging from a rearview mirror. Tangled in a grandmother's purse with the car keys and the cough drops. Laid in someone's hands at a funeral. Some people wear one like a necklace; some call it a lucky charm. People can't even agree how many beads are on it. The string is for something much plainer than luck. It's for counting.
screen: `ON A MIRROR. IN A PURSE.` → `A LUCKY CHARM?` → `IT'S FOR COUNTING.`

segments.voice: Rosary comes from the Latin rosarium, a rose garden: a garland of prayers, like a crown of roses. Here's the layout. A cross, a short tail of beads, then the loop: five sets of ten small beads, called decades, each set apart by a single bead. On the single bead, the Our Father. On each of the ten, a Hail Mary. After each ten, a short line of praise, the Glory Be. One decade on its own takes about five minutes, and plenty of people start there. That's where the arguments about the count come from: fifty-nine beads on the whole string, fifty-three Hail Marys. Counting prayers is ancient. Stories from the early desert monks tell of one who kept track of his daily prayers with pebbles in his lap. Later, monks prayed all one hundred and fifty psalms, and tradition says people who couldn't read prayed one hundred and fifty short prayers instead. The rosary grew out of that, and was called the poor man's psalter. And here's the plain secret. While the fingers and lips are busy with the words, the mind is free to think through scenes from the lives of Jesus and Mary, called the mysteries. That's the real prayer. The beads just keep the hands busy.
screen: `ROSARIUM — A ROSE GARDEN.` · `FIVE DECADES OF TEN.` · `PEBBLES IN A MONK'S LAP.` · `THE MIND ON THE MYSTERIES.`

segments.voice: Three breaths with the bell. Rest one hand in your lap. On each breath out, touch your thumb to the next finger: one, two, three. Don't count out loud. Let the fingers keep track, so the mind doesn't have to.
The rosary. A garland of prayers on a string that keeps count, so the mind can rest on the life of Jesus. Fourth word.
Your line: hands busy, heart free. The beads hold the count, so the mind can go somewhere better. That's day four.

howItsDone: Catholics pray the rosary alone or together, some every day, saying an Our Father, ten Hail Marys and a Glory Be for each decade while thinking about a scene from the life of Jesus and Mary.

story.title: three hundred pebbles
story.text: A monk in the Egyptian desert fills his lap with three hundred pebbles every morning and drops one for each prayer he says. Then he hears of a woman in a village who manages seven hundred a day, and he's crushed. He goes to an old monk named Macarius and confesses it. Macarius tells him he himself says about a hundred, and his conscience is at peace. The count, it turns out, was never the point.

notes: Moved from camp-one day 10 ('the rosary, beads') to day 4 and tightened; the word is now simply 'the rosary' (the Hail Mary keeps its own day, now day 10, with the word 'the Hail Mary'). Title shortened from 'what the string is for (counting, not magic)'.
Bead count, from the audience research's '53 or 59?' question: a standard five-decade rosary has 59 beads (5 on the pendant: 1+3+1; 54 on the loop: 50 + 4) and 53 Hail Marys (3 + 50). Confirm.

The monk with pebbles is Paul of Pherme in Palladius's Lausiac History (ch. 20), 300 prayers a day; the virgin who prayed 700 and Macarius's reply (about 100 prayers, conscience at peace) paraphrased in the story. Confirm.
The 150-prayers origin is framed as 'tradition says'; the Dominic story appears only in the trapdoor as pious tradition. Confirm acceptable to a Catholic Keeper.
Rosary structure simplified (the opening prayers on the tail, such as the Creed, and the Fatima prayer are not described). Confirm.
